title: Provident Tradesmens Bank & Trust Co. v. Patterson (1968)
summary: Rule 19 required a practical assessment of proceeding without the automobile owner, rather than an automatic dismissal based on an indispensable-party label.
notes:
The Court discussed, without deciding, possible effects of the owner’s failure to intervene. Do not convert that discussion into a general rule binding all nonparties who knew of a suit.

The insurer, Lumbermens Mutual Casualty Co., had refused to defend on the theory that Cionci lacked Dutcher's permission; Provident Tradesmens Bank, administrator of passenger Lynch's estate, sought a declaratory judgment that Cionci was a permitted user covered by the policy, and the jury found for the plaintiffs.

The Court identified four interests for the Rule 19(b) inquiry: the plaintiff's interest in a forum, the defendant's interest in avoiding multiple or inconsistent liability, the absent person's interest, and the public and the courts' interest in complete, consistent and efficient settlement of controversies; and it stressed that after a judgment has been rendered the balance shifts because the absent party's interest can be protected by shaping relief.

sections.Parties: The representatives of people killed in an automobile accident and an injured passenger pursued insurance coverage. The owner, Dutcher, was absent from the federal coverage action.
sections.Material Facts: Dutcher lent his car to Cionci. A collision killed Cionci and passengers or other persons and seriously injured Harris. Dutcher’s policy covered permitted drivers and had a $100,000 limit for the accident. The central coverage question was whether Cionci’s use, including an alleged detour, remained permitted. Lynch’s estate held an unpaid $50,000 settlement against Cionci’s penniless estate. The owner shared Pennsylvania citizenship with the plaintiffs, so joining him as a defendant would defeat diversity. His possible personal exposure gave him an interest in preserving the insurance fund.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Harlan, reversed the Third Circuit's judgment and remanded for consideration of the insurer's remaining merits arguments.
sections.Issue: Did the absent owner’s interest require dismissal even after a completed trial, when joining him would destroy diversity?
sections.Holding: No automatic dismissal was warranted. Applying Rule 19(b)’s equity-and-good-conscience inquiry, the court of appeals had erred in discarding the judgment on the grounds it used.
sections.Reasoning: The Court examined the plaintiffs’ interest in retaining their judgment, the insurer’s opportunity to defend, the owner’s actual risk of prejudice, and the public interest in efficient, consistent adjudication. The posture mattered: the investment in a completed trial strengthened the case for preserving the result, and the insurer had not timely asserted a joinder interest. The owner was not automatically bound, but practical depletion of the fund still deserved consideration. Possible protection included withholding payment or limiting total recovery to the policy. The word indispensable described the conclusion reached after this analysis; it could not supply the analysis itself. The Court also rejected the theory that a rigid federal common-law substantive right displaced Rule 19.

learning.why: Rule 19 required a practical assessment of proceeding without the automobile owner, rather than an automatic dismissal based on an indispensable-party label.

topics.cp-required-joinder: The court had to evaluate the actual interests and possible prejudice under Rule 19(b).
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: The inquiry was pragmatic and sensitive to the fact that trial and judgment had already occurred.
topics.cp-diversity: Joining the automobile owner as a defendant would have destroyed diversity.
topics.cp-nonparty-protection: Shaping relief could protect the absent owner without discarding the completed trial.
topics.cp-frcp-19: Provident is the leading Supreme Court reading of the 1966 text of Rule 19(a) and (b).
topics.cp-waiver: The nonjoinder objection was raised for the first time on appeal, and the Court explained why a late-raised Rule 19 objection is weighed differently after judgment.

mnemonic.rationale: A borrowed car and the absent owner
